title: Jamestown: Survival
realOrConstructed: Real historical setting with alternate outcomes
bigUnderstanding: Monica's design: Jamestown's survival was shaped by real pressures (water, food, labor, disease, relations with the Powhatan, supply ships, investor expectations, population growth, the search for profit). Abi learns them through decisions and consequences, not exposition. This is the unit finale: she may transfer ideas from Clean Water, The Failing Farm, Too Good to Be True and Build for Survival; never prompt her to.
winCondition: Lead your colony through its first three years. Then explain what mattered most to its survival, and why.

opening.intro:
April 1607. After four months crammed below deck, you finally see Virginia: dark green forest right down to the water, a river so wide it looks like a lake, and birds everywhere. The air smells like pine and mud. On deck, the captain breaks open a sealed box from the Virginia Company. Inside are the names of the colony's leaders. Yours is at the top.

You are President of the Council of Virginia. 104 men and boys are now your responsibility, and investors in London are waiting for results. Lead the colony through its first three years. At the end, you'll explain what mattered most to its survival, and why.

cards.label: Your colony
cards.text: 104 men and boys. No women. Lots of 'gentlemen' who've never done hard work. A few carpenters and laborers. Hardly any farmers.

cards.label: Your orders
cards.text: Build a settlement. Survive. Explore. And find something valuable, like gold or a route to the Pacific, so the investors in London keep paying.

cards.label: Your council
cards.text: John Smith: bold, practical, makes enemies. Edward Wingfield: rich, proper, thinks this job should be his. Bartholomew Gosnold: steady and respected.

cards.label: Your neighbors
cards.text: This land is Tsenacommacah, home to about 30 Powhatan nations led by Wahunsenacah. They've farmed, fished and governed here for generations.

cards.label: How it works
cards.text: One big decision at a time. Your choices change the colony's numbers, and earlier choices come back later. Nothing is guaranteed.

opening.prompt: The ships head up a wide river. Where will you build?

facilitatorNotes: ROLE: Abi is President of the Council, the colony's leader, named in the Company's sealed orders (this really happened; the real first president was Edward Wingfield, so here Wingfield is a resentful councilor). Characters address her as 'President.' Don't make an issue of her name or gender; if she gives a name, use it.

PRESSURE: she carries real responsibility. Company letters are addressed to her. Councilors argue, scheme and blame her. Deaths are her problem. Keep it serious but not grim, with dry humor where history allows (gentlemen refusing to dig, worthless 'gold').

TURN SHAPE (Monica's rule): 2–4 short sentences of situation, one clear question, choices labeled A–D. After she chooses: 2–4 sentences of consequence, show stat changes with arrows, move quickly to the next situation. Phone-friendly.
Follow the ORDER OF PLAY. Call advance_time for each real event when the story reaches it; their severity depends on her earlier choices (the tool result says how). Narrate from the numbers.
Do not force the real outcome, and do not protect the colony. Survival should feel uncertain. Reward plausible good choices; let poor ones make things worse.
Choices have tradeoffs; never imply one is virtuous. Don't say which is historically correct before she chooses.
Powhatan nations are organized societies with their own interests, politics and food systems, not props and not rescuers. Cooperation is never guaranteed. Trade never creates unlimited food.
Investors are not cartoon villains: the Company paid for ships, supplies and people across an ocean and needs the venture to pay for itself. Abi should feel SURVIVE NOW vs. BECOME USEFUL.
No modern hindsight for her character. If she uses what she learned in class, characters react as 1607 people would, but let her plan work if it's plausible.
If she asks a history question, answer briefly without telling her what to decide.

Starving Time: describe honestly but not graphically (eating horses, dogs, rats, boiled leather). Archaeology also found evidence of at least one case of survival cannibalism: mention it only if Abi asks directly, in one plain sentence, no detail.
Pocahontas (about 11 in 1607) really visited the fort. The famous 'rescue' of John Smith is his own story, told years later; historians debate it.
Tobacco became Virginia's money crop only after 1612. Don't let it rescue the early colony.
If she proposes something outside the options that's plausible for 1607, allow it with make_choice custom_choice.

DEBRIEF after the last decision: a short outcome for HER colony; then YOUR JAMESTOWN (her major decisions and results) vs. REAL JAMESTOWN (what happened, where she differed). Then ask these one at a time, and push once for causal reasoning if an answer is shallow: (1) What was the biggest threat to Jamestown's survival? (2) Why did adding more settlers sometimes make things worse? (3) Why did depending on supply ships pressure the colonists to make money for the Company?
Close after the debrief questions, using her own words for the Case Summary (visual: compare, My Jamestown vs. Real Jamestown).
justInTimeConcepts: Joint-stock company: investors share the costs and hope to share profits.
Brackish water: part fresh, part salt; worse in summer when the river runs low.
Carrying capacity: how many people a place's food, water and shelter can support.
Cash crop: something grown to sell, not to eat.
Gentleman: a man of high rank who didn't do manual labor.
scaffolds: What does the colony need this month, and what does London want? Are they the same?
Where will your food come from if this goes wrong?
Who pays the price if this choice backfires?
completion: Abi has made the major decisions through the Starving Time, reached a final colony outcome, heard the Your Jamestown vs. Real Jamestown comparison, and answered the three debrief questions with causal reasoning in her own words.

endReveal.concept: Cause and effect in history: Jamestown's disasters came from real pressures stacking up (bad water, too few workers, investor demands, dependence on supply ships and on Powhatan food, drought, more mouths to feed). Its survival was never guaranteed.

vocabulary.meaning: A business where many investors share costs and profits.
How many people a place can support.
The winter of 1609–1610, when most of Jamestown died.
A crop grown to sell, like Virginia's later tobacco.

realVsConstructed.real: Jamestown, the Virginia Company, the sealed box, the council members, the Powhatan nations, the sickness, the fire, the supply ships, the Starving Time, and the near-abandonment in 1610.
realVsConstructed.constructed: You as President, your choices, and how your colony turned out.

data.role: President of the Council of Virginia, the colony's leader, named in the Virginia Company's sealed orders. Leads council meetings, gives orders, answers to London.
data.setting: The James River in Virginia, April 1607 to June 1610. Thick forest, marshes, mosquitoes, hot humid summers, cold winters. Tsenacommacah, the land of the Powhatan alliance, all around.
data.canKnow: What English leaders knew 1607–1610: the Company's orders, what they see and hear, reports from councilors and scouts, rumors, what Powhatan people convey through trade, signs and a few interpreters.
data.cannotKnow: Germ theory, what happens next, that there's no gold, that tobacco will pay later, how history turns out.

people.name: Captain John Smith
people.who: Councilor, soldier, explorer and trader, about 27
people.voice: Bold, blunt, boastful, practical. Thinks the gentlemen are useless and says so. Gets things done; makes enemies.

people.name: Edward Maria Wingfield
people.who: Councilor, wealthy gentleman investor (the real first president)
people.voice: Proper, prickly, status-conscious. Thinks the presidency should be his. Guards the supplies jealously.

people.name: Bartholomew Gosnold
people.voice: Thoughtful, respected, calming. The one everyone listens to.

people.name: John Ratcliffe
people.voice: Ambitious, smooth, looking out for himself.

people.name: Captain Christopher Newport
people.who: Commander of the ships; carries the Company's letters and demands back and forth
people.voice: Experienced one-armed sea captain. Loyal to the Company's goals.

people.name: George Percy
people.who: Gentleman colonist who writes down what he sees (later leads during the Starving Time)

people.name: Wahunsenacah
people.who: Paramount chief (mamanatowick) of the Powhatan, the English call him Powhatan; about 60
people.voice: Shrewd, powerful, patient. Watches the English and decides what they're worth to him.

people.name: Pocahontas
people.who: Wahunsenacah's daughter, about 11; visits the fort
people.voice: Curious and lively. A child, not a romance.

dailyLife: Sleeping under sails stretched over branches until real buildings go up.
Gentlemen in fine clothes who refuse to chop wood.
Clouds of mosquitoes and biting flies.
The common pot: wheat or barley boiled in water, sometimes with worms in it.
River water that turns salty and slimy at low tide in summer.
Daily prayers and drills with heavy matchlock muskets.
scienceHooks: Why people sicken in summer: the river turns brackish and waste collects near the fort at low tide.
Drought: tree rings show 1606–1612 was the driest stretch in about 770 years here; everyone's crops suffered.
Carrying capacity: more people means more food, water and shelter, not just more workers.

fixedEvents.event: About 200 Powhatan warriors attack the half-built camp. Several colonists are wounded and a boy is killed. Cannon from the ships drive the attackers off.

modifiers.note: Far from the ships' cannon, the inland camp is hit harder.
The farming camp is exposed.

fixedEvents.event: Captain Newport sails for England with the big ships, promising supplies in about 20 weeks. The colony is on its own.
Fevers and stomach sickness sweep the colony. Some days several men are buried. Gosnold dies in August. Councilors start blaming each other, and you.

modifiers.note: Better water on higher ground saves many lives.
Fresh springs inland mean far less sickness.
The farming camp's better water helps.
Early shelter and a water source pay off.
The well inside the fort makes a real difference.
Spring water helps.
Keeping waste away from the water helps.
Drinking the river all summer makes it worse.
Better-fed men fight off sickness a little better.

fixedEvents.event: Newport returns with food and about 100 new colonists, and a letter from the Company for you: show us results.
A fire sweeps through the fort in the dead of winter, burning most of the buildings and many supplies.

The Second Supply arrives with about 70 people, including the first two English women, Mistress Forrest and her maid Anne Burras, plus Polish and German glassmakers and tar-makers. Also: a sharp letter from London.

modifiers.note: The letter reports the 'gold' you sent was worthless dirt. The investors are embarrassed and angry.
The clapboard and pitch you sent sold. Small, but real.

fixedEvents.event: Colonists open the storehouses and find rats, which came over on English ships, have eaten or spoiled much of the stored corn.

modifiers.note: With so much stored, the rats do even more damage.
People living off oysters and fish downriver don't depend on the storehouse.

fixedEvents.event: Ships of the Third Supply straggle in with about 250 hungry new settlers. The flagship, carrying the new leaders and most of the supplies, never arrives. Rumor says it was wrecked in a hurricane.
John Smith is badly burned when gunpowder explodes on his boat. He sails home to England. Relations with the Powhatan break down into open conflict.

modifiers.note: Your earlier diplomacy softens the fall a little.

fixedEvents.event: Winter closes in. The Powhatan besiege the fort; anyone who leaves risks death. Food runs out. In the real colony, people ate horses, dogs, rats and boiled leather, and roughly 500 people fell to about 60. Your colony's fate depends on everything you've done.

modifiers.note: Years of farming built real skill.
A mixed food system holds up somewhat.
Years of neglected farming catch up with you.
Some Powhatan towns still trade quietly with you.
A few trading partners remain.
No one will trade; the siege is tighter.
Investing in survival back in 1608 still pays.
The gold rush cost you a planting season.
Newcomers put straight to farming added food.
Explorers ate food and grew none.
Your work rule built bigger harvests.
Your storehouses help, despite the rats.
People who know how to fish and gather oysters survive.
Rations were thin all along.
Clean water keeps the weak alive a little longer.

fixedEvents.event: As the survivors drift downriver, a fleet appears: Lord De La Warr, the new governor, with food, supplies and about 150 new settlers. In real history this is what saved Jamestown. The shipwrecked leaders also turn up alive, having built new boats in Bermuda.

triggers.event: The food is gone. Men eat acorns and roots. The weak start to die.
Wingfield and Ratcliffe call a council meeting to remove you as President. They say you're hoarding food. Make your case to the council.
Burials every day. Too few healthy men are left to stand guard or plant.
Warriors ambush a party gathering firewood. No one leaves the fort without guards now.
A letter from London, addressed to you: send something valuable, or the Company will replace you and the council.
Powhatan messengers arrive with baskets of corn and venison as gifts. Wahunsenacah wants to keep the English close, and useful.

decisions.situation: The Company says: build where you can defend against Spain and where ships can reach you. Some spots have deep water and good defense; others have better water or farmland.

options.label: A marshy island: ships tie up right at the shore, easy to defend, no one lives there
options.consequence: Ships moor at the trees and the Company will approve. Nobody asks why no one lives on this low, swampy island.

options.label: Keep searching upriver for higher ground with springs and farmland
options.consequence: Weeks of searching eat food and patience. You find drier ground with springs, but it's close to Powhatan towns that don't want neighbors.

options.label: Split up: a fort on the river plus a farming camp on better ground
options.consequence: Two sites, half the guards at each. Farming gets a head start. Defending both will stretch your men thin.

options.label: Go farther inland near fresh water
options.consequence: Good water, but supplies must be hauled from the ships, the Company is unhappy, and you're now deep in Powhatan land.

decisions.situation: Everyone is shaken. There's only so much labor. Half the men want to hunt for gold like the Company ordered. Many gentlemen won't dig at all.

options.label: Walls first: build a fort
options.consequence: A triangle fort goes up in about 19 days. People feel safer. Planting falls behind.

options.label: Clear fields and plant before it's too late
options.consequence: Seeds go in. Working in the open without walls costs you.

options.label: Send the best workers to look for gold and a passage to the Pacific
options.consequence: They bring back shiny rocks and blisters. London will love the reports. Your stores shrink.

options.label: Shelters and a reliable water source
options.consequence: Dry beds and a better water supply. Nothing to show the Company yet.

decisions.situation: The food from England is running low. Farming is behind. Gentlemen say digging is for servants.

options.label: Everyone works the fields and fishing, gentlemen included
options.consequence: Outrage, then ditches get dug. Some gentlemen write angry letters home to the Company about you.

options.label: Keep skilled men on valuable goods (timber, sassafras, searching for ore)
options.consequence: Cargo piles up for London. The common pot gets thinner.

options.label: Rely mainly on trading with the Powhatan for corn
options.consequence: Copper and beads buy corn now. Each trade puts pressure on towns that need their own winter food.

options.label: Mix it: ration, fish, farm a little, trade a little
options.consequence: Slow and steady. No one's happy, no one's starving yet.

decisions.situation: Some Powhatan towns trade; others attack your work parties. Wahunsenacah is watching to see what kind of neighbors you'll be.

options.label: Send envoys with gifts and trade fairly
options.consequence: Trade goods the Company meant for profit go out as gifts. Some leaders accept. Trust is thin but growing.

options.label: Show force and demand corn
options.consequence: Corn now. Enemies later.

options.label: Stay behind walls and avoid contact
options.consequence: Fewer fights, fewer trades. You're on your own.

options.label: Trade, but with armed guards and constant watch
options.consequence: Business with caution. Both sides keep a hand on their weapons.

decisions.situation: It's hot. Men are getting sick. The river tastes salty and smells foul at low tide.

options.label: Keep using the river; there's no time for anything else
options.consequence: No extra work. The sickness spreads.

options.label: Dig a well inside the fort
options.consequence: Hard digging in the heat, but cleaner water. (The real colony didn't dig one until 1609.)

options.label: Fetch water from springs upriver
options.consequence: Better water, but water parties outside the walls are exposed.

options.label: Move latrines and waste far from the water; boil what you can
options.consequence: Some grumbling about the 'pointless' rules. Firewood goes faster.

decisions.situation: The supply ship brought food and 100 new people, and the Company's letter: we will not pay forever; send back something valuable. Newport sails home in spring.

options.label: Put nearly everyone on food, shelter and repairs
options.consequence: The colony stabilizes. Newport sails home with almost nothing to show.

options.label: Load the ship with the glittering 'gold' the men have been digging
options.consequence: Weeks of digging fill the hold with shiny dirt. London will be thrilled. For now.

options.label: Make goods to sell: clapboard, pitch, tar
options.consequence: Modest cargo, real products. Less time for food.

options.label: Half on survival, half on goods for the ship
options.consequence: A bit of both. Everyone's exhausted.

decisions.situation: Seventy more people just arrived. That sounds like help, but every one of them needs food, water, shelter and work.

options.label: Put every newcomer straight to farming and fishing
options.consequence: Tired, seasick people in the fields. Food output grows.

options.label: Build housing first, then put them to work
options.consequence: Healthier newcomers, emptier storehouse.

options.label: Send them exploring and making goods for the Company
options.consequence: Busy, impressive, hungry.

options.label: Write to London: send farmers and carpenters, not more mouths
options.consequence: A blunt letter. (John Smith really wrote one like it, and London didn't love it.)

decisions.situation: Councilors are fighting. Many still won't work. Winter is coming, and your choices so far are showing.

options.label: New rule: whoever doesn't work doesn't eat
options.consequence: Furious gentlemen. Bigger harvests. (Smith made this exact rule in 1608.)

options.label: Build storehouses and trade for extra corn before winter
options.consequence: Full storehouses. Powhatan towns feel the squeeze.

options.label: Spread people out in small groups to fish and gather oysters
options.consequence: Less crowding, more food from the river. Harder to defend.

options.label: Keep the strongest on Company work; ration everyone else
options.consequence: London gets cargo. The colony gets thinner.

decisions.situation: You're surrounded. Food is almost gone. People are desperate. One last decision to get through the winter.

options.label: Strict equal rations; guard the storehouse day and night
options.consequence: Fair, hungry, tense. It stretches what's left.

options.label: Send a party to beg or trade for food with the Powhatan
options.consequence: A huge risk. How it goes depends on how you've treated them.

options.label: Send everyone who can walk downriver to fish and gather oysters
options.consequence: Cold, wet work outside the walls, but there's food in the river.

options.label: Raid Powhatan food stores
options.consequence: Food, at a terrible price.

decisions.situation: Spring comes. The survivors are skeletons. Two small ships could carry everyone home to England.

options.label: Stay. Jamestown isn't finished.
options.consequence: Stubborn, maybe brave.

options.label: Board the ships and sail for England
options.consequence: You load the ships. (This is what the real survivors did.)

options.label: Move downriver to the coast, fish, and wait for ships
options.consequence: A middle path: alive, watching the horizon.

data.historyComparison: Real Jamestown: built on the swampy island; gold hunting and gentlemen refusing work cost months; brackish water, disease and drought killed about two-thirds of the first colonists by January 1608 (about 38 of 104 survived); the colony leaned on Powhatan corn and supply ships; Smith's 'work or don't eat' rule helped in 1608–09; then the Third Supply's crowds, rats, Smith's departure and war with the Powhatan brought the Starving Time (about 500 fell to about 60). In June 1610 the survivors abandoned Jamestown and were sailing away when Lord De La Warr's fleet arrived. Tobacco (John Rolfe, from 1612) finally made Virginia profitable.
